column1: What is the default-deny principle in firewall design?
column2: All traffic is dropped unless explicitly permitted; the permitted traffic space is enumerated and bounded, rather than trying to enumerate the unbounded space of harmful traffic.

column1: Why does default-deny scale better than default-permit (denylist) models?
column2: Default-deny scales with the number of legitimate services (bounded and knowable), while denylist models scale with the number of threats (unbounded and unknowable).

column1: What is the first-match termination invariant in ACL evaluation?
column2: Rules are evaluated in order, and the first rule whose predicate matches the packet determines the verdict; the system does not compute a union of all matching rules.

column1: What fields constitute the canonical five-tuple used to identify a network flow?
column2: Source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, and protocol.

column1: What problem did stateless packet filters create that stateful inspection solved?
column2: Stateless filters couldn't distinguish legitimate response traffic from unsolicited/spoofed packets on the same ports, forcing admins to either open wide ephemeral port ranges or build complex, incomplete bidirectional rule sets.

column1: What is the directionality invariant in stateful firewalls?
column2: Only explicitly permitted traffic may initiate new connections; response traffic is implicitly permitted via established session state, but attackers cannot forge state by injecting unsolicited responses (e.g., unsolicited SYN-ACKs) since no corresponding outbound request exists.

column1: What is the temporal consistency invariant for stateful firewalls regarding TCP?
column2: The firewall must track actual TCP protocol lifecycle states (SYN_SENT, ESTABLISHED, FIN_WAIT, TIME_WAIT) to distinguish legitimate teardown sequences from malicious packet injection into closed connections.

column1: Why does the perimeter-only firewall model fail against lateral movement?
column2: It treats the network as a binary trust domain (trusted inside / untrusted outside), so once an attacker breaches the perimeter, they gain unrestricted lateral movement with no further policy enforcement points.

column1: What is the purpose of Internal Segmentation Firewalls (ISFWs)?
column2: To enforce default-deny policy at internal trust boundaries (e.g., between DMZ and application tier), containing lateral movement by forcing attackers through additional policy enforcement points.

column1: What are the four architectural invariants common to all firewall designs?
column2: Default-deny, stateful inspection (conntrack-based connection lifecycle tracking), least-privilege routing (minimizing network paths), and (implied) centralized/consistent policy enforcement at trust boundaries.

column1: What is the fundamental limitation of layer 3/4 firewalls that motivates application-layer (DPI) enforcement?
column2: Most security incidents occur in the semantic content of application payloads (e.g., SQL injection in HTTP POST bodies, C2 beacons over HTTPS, DNS tunneling), which header-only inspection at layers 3/4 cannot detect.

column1: Why is application-layer (DPI) inspection computationally far more expensive than stateful packet filtering?
column2: It requires reassembling fragmented/out-of-order packets into full protocol sessions, parsing complex grammars, maintaining multi-exchange application state machines, and evaluating nested policy trees—raising per-packet cost by two to three orders of magnitude versus simple header/hash-table lookups.
